title: Chapter 17 — The Ramadan
paragraphs: Since Queequeg's Ramadan, or day of Fasting and Humiliation, was to continue all day, I decided not to disturb him until nightfall. I have the greatest respect for everyone's religious practices, no matter how odd they might seem. I couldn't bring myself to look down on even a congregation of ants worshipping a toadstool, or those people in certain parts of the world who, with a degree of servility unmatched anywhere else, bow down before the preserved body of a dead landowner simply because of the enormous property still held and rented in his name.

I say, we good Presbyterian Christians should be charitable about these things. We shouldn't consider ourselves so vastly superior to other people — pagans and whoever else — because of their half-crazy ideas on these subjects. There was Queequeg, certainly holding the most absurd beliefs about Yojo and his Ramadan — but so what? Queequeg thought he knew what he was doing, I suppose. He seemed content, and there I should let him be. All our arguing with him wouldn't help. Let him be, I say, and Heaven have mercy on us all — Presbyterians and Pagans alike — for we are all somehow dreadfully cracked in the head and badly need mending.

Toward evening, when I felt sure all his rituals must be over, I went up to his room and knocked on the door. No answer. I tried to open it, but it was locked from inside. "Queequeg," I said softly through the keyhole. All silent. "I say, Queequeg! Why don't you answer? It's me — Ishmael." But everything stayed still as before. I started to worry. I had given him plenty of time. I thought he might have had a stroke. I looked through the keyhole, but since the door opened into an odd corner of the room, the view was narrow and useless. I could only see part of the footboard of the bed and a strip of wall, nothing more. I was surprised to see Queequeg's harpoon shaft leaning against the wall — the landlady had taken it from him the previous evening, before we went up to the room. That's strange, I thought. But since the harpoon was there, and he hardly ever went anywhere without it, he must be inside. No question about it.

"Queequeg! — Queequeg!" — still nothing. Something must have happened. A stroke! I tried to force the door open, but it held firm. Running downstairs, I quickly explained my fears to the first person I met — the chambermaid. "Oh my!" she cried. "I thought something must be wrong. I went to make the bed after breakfast and the door was locked. Not a sound from inside, and it's been just as silent ever since. But I thought maybe you'd both gone out and locked your things in for safekeeping. Oh my! — Ma'am! Murder! Mrs. Hussey! A stroke!" And with those cries she ran toward the kitchen, with me right behind her.
Mrs. Hussey soon appeared, with a mustard pot in one hand and a vinegar bottle in the other, having just been pulled away from setting the table and scolding her little kitchen boy.

"The woodshed!" I cried. "Which way to it? Run, for God's sake, and get something to pry open the door — the axe! The axe! He's had a stroke, I'm sure of it!" And saying this, I was rushing back upstairs empty-handed when Mrs. Hussey blocked my way with the mustard pot, the vinegar bottle, and the full authority of her expression.
"What's the matter with you, young man?"
"Get the axe! For God's sake, someone run for the doctor while I pry it open!"

"Look here," said the landlady, quickly putting down the vinegar bottle to free up a hand. "Look here — are you talking about prying open one of my doors?" And with that she grabbed my arm. "What's the matter with you? What's the matter with you, shipmate?"

As calmly and quickly as I could, I explained the situation. Unconsciously pressing the vinegar bottle against one side of her nose, she thought for a moment, then exclaimed, "No! I haven't seen it since I put it there." Running to a small closet under the stairs, she looked inside, came back, and told me Queequeg's harpoon was missing. "He's killed himself," she cried. "It's that poor Stiggs all over again — there goes another bedspread — God pity his poor mother! It'll be the ruin of my house. Does the poor lad have a sister? Where's that girl? — there, Betty, go to Snarles the Painter, and tell him to paint me a sign: 'No suicides permitted here, and no smoking in the parlor.' Might as well kill both birds at once. Kill? The Lord be merciful to his ghost! What's that noise up there? You, young man, stop right there!"
And running up after me, she caught me as I was again trying to force the door open.

"I won't allow it. I won't have my property damaged. Go for the locksmith — there's one about a mile from here. But wait —" putting her hand in her pocket — "here's a key that might fit; let's see." She turned it in the lock. But Queequeg's bolt on the inside was still thrown.

"Have to break it down," I said, and was running back down the hall to get a running start when the landlady grabbed me again, insisting I not break down her property. But I tore free and, with a sudden full-body charge, threw myself against the door.

With a tremendous crash the door flew open, the knob slamming into the wall and sending plaster to the ceiling. And there — good heavens! — there sat Queequeg, perfectly cool and composed, right in the middle of the room, squatting on his heels, holding Yojo on top of his head. He looked neither one way nor the other but sat like a carved statue with barely a sign of life.
"Queequeg," I said, going up to him, "Queequeg, what's the matter with you?"
"He hasn't been sitting like that all day, has he?" said the landlady.

But no matter what we said, we couldn't drag a single word out of him. I almost felt like pushing him over just to change his position, which was almost unbearable to look at — so painfully and unnaturally stiff. Especially since, in all likelihood, he had been sitting that way for eight or ten hours, going without his regular meals the whole time.
"Mrs. Hussey," said I, "he's alive, at any rate. So leave us, please, and I'll deal with this strange business myself."

Closing the door on the landlady, I tried to get Queequeg to sit in a chair, but it was useless. There he sat. Despite all my polite efforts and coaxing, he wouldn't budge an inch, say a single word, look at me, or show the slightest awareness that I was there.

I wonder, I thought, if this could be part of his Ramadan. Do they fast while squatting like this on his native island? It must be so. Yes, it's part of his religion, I suppose. Well, let him be. He'll get up sooner or later. It can't last forever, thank God. And his Ramadan only comes once a year — and I don't think it's very punctual even then.

I went down to supper. After sitting a long time listening to the rambling stories of some sailors who had just come from a "plum-pudding voyage," as they called it — meaning a short whaling trip in a schooner or brig, limited to waters north of the equator in the Atlantic Ocean — after listening to these plum-puddingers until nearly eleven o'clock, I went upstairs to bed, feeling quite sure by then that Queequeg must have finished his Ramadan. But no — there he was, exactly where I had left him. He hadn't moved an inch. I started getting annoyed with him. It seemed so utterly senseless and insane to sit there all day and half the night on his heels in a cold room, holding a piece of wood on his head.
"For heaven's sake, Queequeg, get up and move around. Get up and have some supper. You'll starve. You'll kill yourself, Queequeg." But not a word did he reply.

Giving up on him, I decided to go to bed and sleep. No doubt he would follow before long. But before turning in, I took my heavy bearskin jacket and threw it over him, since it promised to be a very cold night and he had nothing but his ordinary light jacket on. For some time, no matter what I did, I couldn't fall asleep. I had blown out the candle, and the mere thought of Queequeg — not four feet away — sitting in that miserable position, completely alone in the cold and dark — it made me truly wretched. Think of it: sleeping all night in the same room with a wide-awake pagan squatting in this dreary, inexplicable Ramadan!

But somehow I drifted off at last and knew nothing more until daybreak. Looking over the side of the bed, there squatted Queequeg, as if he had been bolted to the floor. But as soon as the first rays of sun entered the window, up he got, with stiff and creaking joints but a cheerful face. He limped over to where I lay, pressed his forehead against mine, and said his Ramadan was over.

Now, as I mentioned before, I have no objection to anyone's religion, whatever it may be, as long as that person doesn't kill or insult anyone else for not sharing it. But when a person's religion becomes truly fanatical — when it's a source of real torment, and when, in short, it makes this earth of ours an uncomfortable place to live — then I think it's high time to take that individual aside and have a serious talk.

And that's exactly what I did with Queequeg. "Queequeg," I said, "get into bed and lie down and listen to me." I then launched into a review, beginning with the rise and development of primitive religions and working my way down to the various religions of today. Throughout, I tried to show Queequeg that all these Lents, Ramadans, and long hours of squatting in cold, cheerless rooms were complete nonsense — bad for the health, useless for the soul, and contrary to the basic laws of hygiene and common sense. I told him that since he was in other respects such an extremely sensible and wise person, it pained me — deeply pained me — to see him being so foolish about this ridiculous Ramadan of his. Besides, I argued, fasting weakens the body, which weakens the spirit, and all thoughts born of fasting are necessarily half-starved. This is why most sickly religious people hold such gloomy ideas about the afterlife. In a word, Queequeg, I said, getting somewhat off track: hell is an idea first born from an undigested apple dumpling, and has been perpetuated ever since through the hereditary indigestion caused by Ramadans.

I then asked Queequeg whether he himself was ever troubled with indigestion, putting the question very plainly so he could understand. He said no — except on one memorable occasion. It was after a great feast given by his father, the king, celebrating a great battle in which fifty of the enemy had been killed by about two in the afternoon and all cooked and eaten that very evening.

"No more, Queequeg," I said, shuddering. "That will do." I knew what he was implying without him spelling it out. I had met a sailor who had visited that very island, and he told me that when a great battle was won there, the custom was to barbecue all the slain in the victor's yard or garden. Then, one by one, they were placed on great wooden platters, garnished around like a pilaf with breadfruit and coconuts, and with parsley in their mouths, were sent round with the victor's compliments to all his friends — just as though these gifts were so many Christmas turkeys.

In the end, I don't think my remarks about religion made much of an impression on Queequeg. In the first place, he seemed somewhat deaf to that particular subject, unless it was approached from his own point of view. In the second place, he didn't understand more than a third of what I said, no matter how simply I put it. And finally, he no doubt believed he knew a good deal more about true religion than I did. He looked at me with a sort of condescending pity and compassion, as though he thought it a great shame that such a sensible young man should be so hopelessly lost to proper pagan devotion.

At last we got up and dressed. Queequeg ate a tremendously hearty breakfast of chowders of every kind, making sure the landlady wouldn't profit too much from his Ramadan. Then we headed out to board the Pequod, strolling along and picking our teeth with halibut bones.
